items.title: Parabolic cylinder and parabolic boundary
items.statement:
Let $n\ge1$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be a nonempty bounded open set with
closure $\overline\Omega$ and boundary $\partial\Omega$ in the sense of
[[def-metric-interior-closure-boundary]], and let $T>0$. Write
$Q:=\Omega\times(0,T]$ for the **space-time cylinder** and
$$\overline Q:=\overline\Omega\times[0,T]\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+1}$$
for its closure in the space-time variable; the **final-time face** is
$\Omega\times\{T\}$, while the **parabolic boundary** of $Q$ is
$$\partial_pQ:=(\overline\Omega\times\{0\})\cup(\partial\Omega\times[0,T]).$$
No point of the final-time face belongs to $\partial_pQ$: the intersections
$\bigl(\Omega\times\{T\}\bigr)\cap\bigl(\overline\Omega\times\{0\}\bigr)$ and
$\bigl(\Omega\times\{T\}\bigr)\cap\bigl(\partial\Omega\times[0,T]\bigr)$ are
empty because $T>0$ and $\Omega\cap\partial\Omega=\varnothing$.

A function $u$ on $\overline Q$ is of class $C^{2,1}(\overline Q)$ if it is
continuous there, is $C^2$ in $x$ and $C^1$ in $t$ on $Q$, and the functions
$u_t$ and $D_x^\alpha u$ for $|\alpha|\le2$ extend continuously to
$\overline Q$; the multi-index notation and the classes $C^k$ are those of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], and at $t=T$ the time
derivative means the left one-sided limit. The relevant operator is
$\partial_t-\Delta_x$, the heat operator of
[[def-heat-equation-heat-operator-and-cauchy-problem]], and the phrase
"$u_t-\Delta u\le0$ in $Q$" always refers to that cylinder, with the one-sided
interpretation of $u_t$ on the final-time face.

On this page a **classical heat solution** means a function with the stated $C^{2,1}$ regularity satisfying the equation pointwise; no second time derivative is required. Formulas that put time first use the canonical coordinate permutation $(x,t)\leftrightarrow(t,x)$; regularity and derivatives always refer to the named spatial and time variables. The analogous interior class has the same continuous derivatives without an up-to-boundary requirement.

Two elementary topological facts are part of the vocabulary. First,
$\overline Q$ is compact: $\Omega$ is bounded, so $\overline\Omega$ is closed and
bounded in $\mathbb R^n$, hence compact ([[thm-heine-borel-rn]]); then
$\overline Q=\overline\Omega\times[0,T]$ is closed and bounded in
$\mathbb R^{n+1}$, hence compact by the same theorem
([[def-metric-compactness]]). Second, $\partial_pQ$ is closed in
$\mathbb R^{n+1}$, being the union of the two closed sets
$\overline\Omega\times\{0\}$ and $\partial\Omega\times[0,T]$; in particular it
is a closed subset of $\overline Q$
([[def-metric-interior-closure-boundary]]).
items.strategy: Definition and remarks: Q is half-open in time, with compact closure and closed initial/lateral parabolic boundary. T>0 and openness of Omega exclude the final spatial-interior face from that boundary. The named C^{2,1} convention is anisotropic and requires only a left time derivative at T, explicitly differing from the earlier isotropic C2 vocabulary. No boundary smoothness or connectedness is imposed; coordinate permutation is explicit.

items.title: The Hessian is negative semidefinite at an interior local maximum
items.statement:
Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f\in C^2(U)$, and let $a\in U$ be a
local maximum of $f$. Then
$$h^{\mathsf T}H_f(a)h\le0\qquad\text{for every }h\in\mathbb R^n;$$
in particular $\nabla f(a)=0$ and $\Delta f(a)=\operatorname{tr}H_f(a)\le0$.
items.strategy: Statement and steps 1.1–3.1: Fermat removes the linear Taylor term. A positive directional quadratic form would exceed the local maximum for small nonzero t, so every form value is nonpositive; h=0 causes no division. Coordinate vectors then give trace<=0. n>=1 is explicit. The result is semidefiniteness, with no strict negativity or converse asserted; the secondary bibliography description no longer claims a false stronger sign.

items.title: Strict-subsolution perturbation for the heat operator
items.statement:
Let $Q=\Omega\times(0,T]$ be a parabolic cylinder ([[def-parabolic-cylinder-and-parabolic-boundary]]) with $\Omega$ bounded, and let $u\in C^{2,1}(\overline Q)$ satisfy $u_t-\Delta u\le0$ in $Q$. Then:

(i) for every $\varepsilon>0$ the function $v:=u+\varepsilon|x|^2$ is in $C^{2,1}(\overline Q)$ and satisfies
$$v_t-\Delta v\le-2n\varepsilon<0\qquad\text{in }Q;$$

(ii) if $w\in C^{2,1}(\overline Q)$ satisfies $w_t-\Delta w<0$ in $Q$, then $\max_{\overline Q}w=\max_{\partial_pQ}w$.
items.strategy:
(i) For $|x|^2=\langle x,x\rangle$ one computes $\partial_ix_j=\delta_{ij}$, $\partial_i|x|^2=2x_i$ and $\partial_i\partial_i|x|^2=2$ by the chain and product rules ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-chain-rule]], [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]); summing over $i$ gives $\Delta|x|^2=2n$ ([[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]). Since $v_t=u_t$ and $\Delta v=\Delta u+2n\varepsilon$, the claim follows by linearity.

(ii) Suppose the maximum of $w$ over the compact set $\overline Q$ ([[thm-heine-borel-rn]], [[def-metric-compactness]]) is attained at a point $P\notin\partial_pQ$; write $P=(x_0,t_0)$. Then $x_0\in\Omega$ and $0<t_0\le T$. If $t_0<T$ then $P$ is an interior point of $Q$ in both variables, so Fermat's interior-extremum theorem in the time variable ([[thm-fermat-interior-extremum]]) gives $w_t(P)=0$, while the spatial maximum gives $w_{x_ix_j}(P)$ negative semidefinite and hence $\Delta w(P)\le0$ by [[lem-negative-semidefinite-hessian-at-an-interior-local-maximum]]; then $(w_t-\Delta w)(P)\ge0$, contradicting $w_t-\Delta w<0$. If $t_0=T$, the left difference quotients $\bigl(w(x_0,T)-w(x_0,T-h)\bigr)/h$ are $\ge0$ because $w$ is maximised at $t=T$, and by the mean value theorem ([[cor-mean-value-theorem]]) and continuity of $w_t$ up to the top face they converge to $w_t(x_0,T)$; hence $w_t(x_0,T)\ge0$, while $\Delta w(x_0,T)\le0$ as before, again contradicting $w_t-\Delta w<0$. So the maximum is attained on $\partial_pQ$. Both parts are pointwise estimates; only finitely many points and parameters are chosen and no choice principle is used.

items.title: Weak parabolic maximum principle
items.statement:
Let $Q=\Omega\times(0,T]$ be a parabolic cylinder with $\Omega$ bounded, and let $u\in C^{2,1}(\overline Q)$ satisfy $u_t-\Delta u\le0$ in $Q$. Then
$$\max_{\overline Q}u=\max_{\partial_pQ}u.$$
items.strategy:
For $\varepsilon>0$ put $v:=u+\varepsilon|x|^2$. By [[lem-strict-subsolution-perturbation-for-the-heat-operator]](i) $v$ is a $C^{2,1}(\overline Q)$ strict subsolution, and by (ii) its maximum over $\overline Q$ is attained on $\partial_pQ$. Since $\Omega$ is bounded, $R^2:=\sup_{x\in\overline\Omega}|x|^2<\infty$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]). Hence
$$\max_{\overline Q}u\le\max_{\overline Q}v=\max_{\partial_pQ}v\le\max_{\partial_pQ}u+\varepsilon R^2 .$$
The right-hand side tends to $\max_{\partial_pQ}u$ as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ by the Archimedean property ([[thm-of-archimedean]]), so $\max_{\overline Q}u\le\max_{\partial_pQ}u$; the reverse inequality is immediate since $\partial_pQ\subseteq\overline Q$. Both maxima exist by compactness and continuity ([[thm-heine-borel-rn]], [[def-metric-compactness]], [[thm-extreme-value-metric]]). The perturbation argument quantifies over $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$ and no choice principle is used.

items.title: Heat balls and their time slices
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge1$, and let $\Gamma$ be the heat kernel of
[[def-heat-kernel]], with $|x-y|^2=\langle x-y,x-y\rangle$ the Euclidean square
of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. For a space-time point $P=(x,t)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R$
and $r>0$ the **heat ball** is
$$E_r(t,x)=E_r(P):=\{(y,s)\in\mathbb R^{n+1}:s<t,\ \Gamma(x-y,t-s)\ge r^{-n}\}\cup\{(x,t)\}.$$
Write $\tau:=t-s$ for the time depth below the top point. Record the following
facts.

(i) $E_r(t,x)$ is compact, and $(x,t)$ is its unique point of maximal time;

(ii) for $0<\tau<r^2/(4\pi)$ the time slice is the closed ball
$$\{y:(y,t-\tau)\in E_r(t,x)\}=\overline B\bigl(x,\rho_n(\tau)\bigr),\qquad \rho_n(\tau):=\sqrt{2n\tau\log\tfrac{r^2}{4\pi\tau}},$$
the slice at $\tau=r^2/(4\pi)$ is the single point $\{x\}$, and the slice is
empty for $\tau>r^2/(4\pi)$; the function $\rho_n$ is continuous on
$(0,r^2/4\pi)$ and $\rho_n(\tau)\to0$ as $\tau\downarrow0$;

(iii) $\displaystyle\sup_{0<\tau<r^2/4\pi}\rho_n(\tau)=\frac r2\sqrt{\frac{2n}{\pi e}}$,
attained at $\tau=r^2/(4\pi e)$, so
$E_r(t,x)\subseteq\overline B\bigl(x,\tfrac r2\sqrt{2n/\pi e}\bigr)\times[t-r^2/4\pi,t]$;

(iv) the boundary is
$\partial E_r(t,x)=\{(y,s):s<t,\ \Gamma(x-y,t-s)=r^{-n}\}\cup\{(x,t)\}$, and on
the level set $\Gamma=r^{-n}$ the gradient of $\Gamma$ is nowhere zero, so that
level set is a $C^\infty$ hypersurface.
items.strategy: Definition (i)–(iv) and remarks: logarithmic algebra gives closed slices, the lower singleton and no later-depth slice. Differentiating tau log(a/tau) gives maximum at a/e and radius r sqrt(n/(2 pi e)); exponential decay gives the zero-radius top limit. The set is closed and bounded. At y=x the nonzero time derivative supplies the regular level even at the lower tip; the implicit-function theorem applies below the top. The top is a nonisolated boundary point, not part of the smooth level. Spatial-first point coordinates agree with Q; n=1 is included.

items.title: Heat-ball representation formula
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $u$ be of class $C^{2,1}$ on a neighbourhood of the
closed heat ball $E:=E_r(t,x)$ of [[def-heat-ball-and-its-slices]], and put
$f:=u_t-\Delta u$. Then, with $\rho_n$ the slice radius,
$$u(x,t)=\iint_E\bigl(\Gamma(x-y,t-s)-r^{-n}\bigr)f(y,s)\,dy\,ds+\frac{1}{2r^n}\int_{t-r^2/4\pi}^{t}\frac{\rho_n(t-s)}{t-s}\int_{|y-x|=\rho_n(t-s)}u(y,s)\,dS(y)\,ds,$$
all integrals absolutely convergent. For $n=1$, the inner sphere integral is the sum over its two points; endpoint slices are irrelevant to the time integral.
items.strategy: Statement and steps 1.1–5.1: convolution in all n+1 variables approximates u, ut and its spatial derivatives uniformly near the compact ball without demanding mixed derivatives. For smooth u, the truncated domain has a regular lower tip and transverse cap; div(u grad v-v grad u,uv)=v f because vs+Delta v=0. The outward lateral normal supplies the negative flux; its Gram-factor cancellation gives R/(2 r^n tau) times the sphere integral. Cap Gaussian mass tends to one while the constant subtraction tends to zero. Volume domination uses int_E Gamma<=r^2/(4 pi); lateral domination reduces to exp(-nq/2) q^(n/2), integrable at both ends. n=1 uses counting measure. Uniform approximation then proves exactly the C^{2,1} assertion. Amended F1's top-point coordinate typo from (t,x) to (x,t), closed defect f39-b1-coordinate-typing. No Statement change.

items.title: Submean inequality for heat subsolutions on heat balls
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $u$ be of class $C^{2,1}$ on a neighbourhood of the
closed heat ball $E_r(t,x)$ of [[def-heat-ball-and-its-slices]] and suppose
$u_t-\Delta u\le0$ there. Then
$$u(x,t)\le\frac{1}{2r^n}\int_{t-r^2/4\pi}^{t}\frac{\rho_n(t-s)}{t-s}\int_{|y-x|=\rho_n(t-s)}u(y,s)\,dS(y)\,ds .$$
In particular, if $u\le M$ on $E_r(t,x)$ then $u(x,t)\le M$.
items.strategy: Statement and steps 1.1–3.1: the representation's volume kernel is nonnegative below its measure-zero top, while f<=0, so dropping its integral gives the stated upper average. Applying the checked representation to a constant normalizes the lateral weight to one, including n=1 and negative M. The same original C^{2,1}-near-ball hypothesis is retained. Brezis is accurately described as an alternative maximum-principle proof, not as a source of this heat-ball inequality.

items.title: Heat-ball chains reach earlier points
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let
$0<t_1<t_0\le T<\infty$, and let $\gamma:[0,1]\to\Omega$ be a Lipschitz path
with compact image $K$. Then there is $\rho>0$ such that
$E_\rho(P)\subseteq\Omega\times(0,T]$ for every $P\in K\times[t_1,t_0]$, and for
every $s\in[t_1,t_0)$ there are $N\ge1$ and points
$P_0=(\gamma(0),t_0),P_1,\dots,P_N=(\gamma(1),s)$, all lying in
$K\times[t_1,t_0]$, with $P_{j+1}\in E_\rho(P_j)$ for all $0\le j<N$.
items.strategy: Statement and steps 1.1–4.1: distance to the nonempty complement is 1-Lipschitz and positive on K, so its attained minimum is positive; the whole-space case explicitly takes d=1. A fixed rho smaller than this distance and sqrt(4 pi t1) encloses every heat ball. Dividing time t0-s and the Lipschitz path into N pieces makes displacement at most L/N; the sufficient logarithmic inequality is stronger than the exact N-multiplied slice condition and holds for sufficiently large N. Constant paths, s=t1, t0=T and n=1 are included; s=t0 is excluded as stated.

items.title: Strong parabolic maximum principle
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $Q=\Omega\times(0,T]$ be a parabolic cylinder
with $\Omega$ bounded, let $u\in C^{2,1}(\overline Q)$ satisfy
$u_t-\Delta u\le0$ in $Q$, and suppose the maximum $M:=\max_{\overline Q}u$ is
attained at a point $(x_0,t_0)$ with $x_0\in\Omega$ and $0<t_0\le T$. Let
$\Omega_0$ be the connected component of $\Omega$ containing $x_0$. Then
$$u=M\quad\text{on }\Omega_0\times(0,t_0].$$
items.strategy: Statement and steps 1.1–4.1: the normalized positive lateral measure has full support in sphere-time charts (counting measure for n=1), so equality at a maximum forces equality on the lateral level and, by continuity, its lower tip. Smaller heat-ball levels fill the interior. At t=T translated balls lie in strictly positive interior time, and compact uniform continuity passes their submean inequalities to the top without an extension beyond T. The checked path-chain lemma then propagates to every earlier point of the same component; time continuity gives t0. There is no propagation to later times or other components. Corrected remaining reversed slots in F1, F3 and the translated supremum of step 1.1 to spatial-first u(y,s) and (y,s); closed defect f39-b1-strong-coordinate-typing. No Statement change.

items.title: Strict positivity propagates to later interior times
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega$ be bounded and connected and
$u\in C^{2,1}(\overline\Omega\times[0,T])$ be a nonnegative homogeneous heat
solution. If $u(x_*,s_*)>0$ at an interior point with $0<s_*<T$, then
$u(x,t)>0$ for every $x\in\Omega$ and $s_*<t\le T$. The same conclusion for
every $0<t\le T$ holds if the continuous initial trace is positive at some interior
point. Nontriviality only at a later time does not assert positivity before
that time.
items.strategy: Statement and steps 1.1–3.1: if a later interior zero occurred, -u would attain global maximum zero on the truncated cylinder. The checked strong principle and connectedness would force u to vanish at the earlier positive point, a contradiction. A positive initial interior trace gives a positive point at a sufficiently small s*<t by continuity. The range is exactly 0<t<=T, and positivity observed later makes no assertion for earlier times or boundary values.

items.title: Comparison and uniqueness for the bounded-cylinder heat problem
items.statement:
Let $Q=\Omega\times(0,T]$ be a parabolic cylinder with $\Omega$ bounded.

(i) If $u,v\in C^{2,1}(\overline Q)$ satisfy $u_t-\Delta u\le v_t-\Delta v$ in $Q$ and $u\le v$ on $\partial_pQ$, then $u\le v$ on $\overline Q$.

(ii) If $f\in C(Q)$ and $g\in C(\partial_pQ)$ are real-valued, then there is at most one $u\in C^{2,1}(\overline Q)$ with $u_t-\Delta u=f$ in $Q$ and $u=g$ on $\partial_pQ$.
items.strategy:
(i) The operator is linear: $w:=u-v$ satisfies $w_t-\Delta w=(u_t-\Delta u)-(v_t-\Delta v)\le0$ in $Q$ ([[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]), and $w\le0$ on $\partial_pQ$. By the weak maximum principle [[thm-weak-parabolic-maximum-principle]], $\max_{\overline Q}w\le\max_{\partial_pQ}w\le0$.

(ii) If $u_1,u_2$ are two solutions with the same $f$ and $g$, their difference $w$ satisfies $w_t-\Delta w=0$ and $w=0$ on $\partial_pQ$; part (i) applied to the pairs $(w,0)$ and $(0,w)$ gives $w\le0$ and $w\ge0$, so $w\equiv0$. No choice principle beyond the weak maximum principle's suppliers is used.

items.title: Supremum norm stability for forced heat problems
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty, bounded and open, $T>0$, and let real
$u,v\in C^{2,1}(\overline\Omega\times[0,T])$ solve $u_t-\Delta u=f$,
$v_t-\Delta v=g$ with $f,g\in C(\overline\Omega\times[0,T])$. Put
$a=\|u(\cdot,0)-v(\cdot,0)\|_\infty$,
$b_t=\sup_{\partial\Omega\times[0,t]}|u-v|$, and
$m(s)=\max_{\overline\Omega}|f(\cdot,s)-g(\cdot,s)|$. Then for $0<t\le T$,
$$\sup_{\overline\Omega\times[0,t]}|u-v|\le\max(a,b_t)+\int_0^t m(s)ds,$$
and hence also the bound with $a+b_t$ in place of the maximum.
items.strategy: Statement and steps 1.1–4.1: nonempty bounded open Omega and continuous closed-cylinder forcing supply each maximum m(s); uniform continuity gives |m(s)-m(s0)|<=sup_x |(f-g)(x,s)-(f-g)(x,s0)|. FTC makes +/-[max(a,b_t)+int_0^s m] admissible C^{2,1} barriers with zero spatial Laplacian. Comparing both signs bounds the difference throughout the truncated cylinder; nonnegativity of m gives the desired supremum. The sharper max(a,b_t) and weaker a+b_t bounds are both sound; zero forcing, a=b_t=0 and t=T are included.

items.title: Energy uniqueness for the homogeneous heat equation
items.statement:
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $n\ge2$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be a
bounded $C^1$ domain (or belong to the specified finite piecewise $C^1$ class)
of [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]], let $T>0$,
and let $u\in C^{2,1}(\overline Q)$ solve $u_t-\Delta u=0$ in
$Q=\Omega\times(0,T]$ with $u=0$ on $\partial\Omega\times[0,T]$ and
$u(\cdot,0)=0$ on $\Omega$. Then $u\equiv0$ on $\overline Q$; equivalently, the
Dirichlet problem for the homogeneous heat equation is unique in this class by
the energy method. No backward-in-time or terminal-data uniqueness is claimed
here (the time-reversed function solves the backward heat equation, for which
the energy is nondecreasing rather than nonincreasing).
items.strategy: Statement and steps 1.1–4.1: the real energy argument matches the n>=2 C1/piecewise C1 Green supplier. Compact bounded derivatives and finite-volume domain justify differentiation and endpoint continuity. Zero lateral values eliminate the Green term, E'<=0 propagates E(0)=0, and positive-volume boxes turn zero energy into pointwise zero before closure continuity. The same reasoning applies componentwise if complex-valued solutions are intended. This proves forward uniqueness only; no terminal-data argument is used.

items.title: Energy identity for the forced Dirichlet heat equation
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge2$ and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a
bounded $C^1$ domain in the class of the first Green identity
([[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]), let $T>0$,
and let real $u\in C^{2,1}(\overline\Omega\times[0,T])$ solve
$u_t-\Delta u=f$ in $\Omega\times(0,T]$ with $f\in C(\overline\Omega\times[0,T])$ and $u=0$ on the
lateral boundary $\partial\Omega\times[0,T]$. Then for $0<t<T$,
$$\frac12\frac d{dt}\int_\Omega u(x,t)^2\,dx+\int_\Omega|Du(x,t)|^2\,dx=\int_\Omega f(x,t)u(x,t)\,dx ,$$
and integrating in $t$ gives the energy balance
$$\frac12\int_\Omega u(x,t_2)^2dx-\frac12\int_\Omega u(x,t_1)^2dx+\int_{t_1}^{t_2}\!\int_\Omega|Du|^2\,dx\,dt=\int_{t_1}^{t_2}\!\int_\Omega fu\,dx\,dt$$
for $0<t_1<t_2<T$. The identity carries exactly the Countable Choice assumption
of the Green identity supplier.
items.strategy: Statement and steps 1.1–3.1: n>=2 and the bounded C1 domain match Green's exact domain class. Continuous extensions give bounded u, ut and gradient, and a containing box gives finite volume. Differentiation under the integral and Green's identity with v=u yield E'+int |Du|^2=int fu with zero lateral term. Dominated convergence makes each time integral continuous before FTC on interior t1,t2. Disconnected domains and f=0 are allowed; endpoint identities are not overclaimed.

items.title: Backward uniqueness for the heat equation on a bounded interval
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $T>0$, $Q=(0,\pi)\times(0,T]$, and say that a
function $w:\overline Q\to\mathbb R$ is of class $C^{4,2}(\overline Q)$ when it
is continuous on $\overline Q$ and all ordered partial derivatives containing at most four $x$ derivatives and at most two $t$ derivatives exist on $Q$ and
extend continuously to $\overline Q$. Suppose $w\in C^{4,2}(\overline Q)$
satisfies
$$w_t=w_{xx}\quad\text{in }Q,\qquad w(0,t)=w(\pi,t)=0\ (0\le t\le T),\qquad w(x,T)=0\ (0\le x\le\pi).$$
Then $w\equiv0$ on $\overline Q$. **No hypothesis on the initial face $t=0$ is
imposed**: the vanishing is forced by the lateral and terminal conditions alone.
Consequently two solutions of the interval Dirichlet problem in this class with
zero lateral data and the same terminal data coincide, and the terminal-to-initial
map is well defined on the class of terminal data of such solutions.
items.strategy: Statement and steps 1.1–5.1: the stated ordered C^{4,2} derivatives justify differentiating the energy twice. Boundary time derivatives vanish by the time-integral identity passed to spatial endpoints. Integration by parts yields E'=-int wx^2 and E''=2 int wt^2; Cauchy–Schwarz gives E'^2<=E E''. Monotonicity and continuity reduce any positive energy, including at time zero, to an interior t0 and first later zero b. Convexity of log E with fixed s<t0 contradicts log E(t)->-infinity at b. Zero energy gives pointwise vanishing, and the difference argument proves the terminal map is well defined without initial data.

references.locator: §6.4, printed pp. 162–163, Theorem 6.21 (backwards uniqueness) and its proof: log-convexity of the energy via $\dot E^2\le E\ddot E$, the maximal positivity interval, and the endpoint limit. The scaffold removes Teschl's initial-face hypothesis and tracks the differentiability class explicitly.

items.title: The Duhamel heat potential
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge1$, $T>0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and let
$f:[0,T]\to L^p(\mathbb R^n)$ be continuous, where $L^p$ is the quotient space
of [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]. For $0\le t\le T$ the
**heat potential** of $f$ is the Bochner integral
$$Df(t):=\int_0^tH_{t-s}f(s)\,ds\ \in\ L^p(\mathbb R^n),$$
where $H$ is the heat evolution of [[def-heat-evolution-of-initial-data]] and
the integrand is the $L^p$-valued function $s\mapsto H_{t-s}f(s)$ interpreted
as in [[def-bochner-integrable-function]] and
[[def-strongly-measurable-banach-valued-function]].

**Well-definedness.** The target $L^p$ is Banach by [[thm-riesz-fischer-completeness-of-l-p]] under the declared Countable Choice. For $1\le p<\infty$ the map $s\mapsto H_{t-s}f(s)$ is
norm continuous on $[0,t]$ as a composition of the continuous curve $f$ and the
strongly continuous heat flow [[thm-heat-cauchy-solution-for-lp-data]]; its
range is therefore separable. For $p=\infty$ strong continuity at time zero is
not available, but the flow is norm continuous on every compact subinterval of
$(0,\infty)$ by the $L^1$ continuity of the positive-time kernels
(for $a\le\tau\le b$ the explicit kernels converge pointwise with a common integrable Gaussian majorant, so [[thm-dominated-convergence]] gives $L^1$ continuity, and Young gives operator-norm continuity),
so for fixed $t$ the integrand is norm continuous on every compact subinterval
of $[0,t)$ and may be approximated on a countable exhaustion of $[0,t)$ by
finite-valued mesh functions, extended by zero on the omitted tail; uniform mesh error at most $1/k$ on $[0,t-t/(k+1)]$ gives pointwise convergence at every $s<t$; the single endpoint value at $s=t$ is
irrelevant for the integral. In both cases the integrand is strongly measurable,
and the contraction estimate of
[[cor-heat-flow-is-order-preserving-and-lp-contractive]] gives
$\|H_{t-s}f(s)\|_p\le\|f(s)\|_p$, so
$$\int_0^t\|H_{t-s}f(s)\|_p\,ds\le\int_0^t\|f(s)\|_p\,ds\le T\sup_{[0,T]}\|f\|_p<\infty .$$
The Bochner integrability criterion [[thm-bochner-integrability-criterion]]
therefore makes $Df(t)$ a well-defined element of $L^p(\mathbb R^n)$, and the
norm inequality for Bochner integrals
[[lem-bochner-integral-norm-inequality]] gives the estimate
$$\|Df(t)\|_p\le\int_0^t\|f(s)\|_p\,ds .$$

The same definition is used when $f$ is merely strongly measurable with
$\int_0^T\|f(s)\|_p\,ds<\infty$ and $1\le p<\infty$: approximation by measurable finite-valued simple functions together with the contraction bound gives strong measurability of the integrand: for the $k$-th simple approximation, replace its finitely many positive-time flow curves by finite mesh functions with error at most $1/k$ on $[0,t-t/(k+1)]$, and put zero on the omitted tail. At every $s<t$ off the original null set the resulting simple functions converge to $H_{t-s}f(s)$ ([[def-strongly-measurable-banach-valued-function]],
[[thm-dominated-convergence]]), and the criterion and estimate above apply
verbatim.

When $f:\mathbb R^n\times[0,T]\to\mathbb R$ is bounded and jointly continuous,
the **scalar heat potential** is
$$u(t,x):=\int_0^t\int_{\mathbb R^n}\Gamma(x-y,t-s)f(y,s)\,dy\,ds,$$
a scalar potential defined by the convolution
[[def-convolution-of-two-functions-on-rn]]; the inner integral is absolutely
convergent because $\Gamma(\cdot,t-s)$ has unit mass
[[lem-heat-kernel-normalisation-scaling-and-derivatives]] and $f$ is bounded.
Whenever the forcing also defines a Bochner integrable $L^p$-valued map, the
scalar potential agrees with the Bochner potential almost everywhere. Indeed, for any bounded measurable test function $\psi$ supported in a bounded set, the pairing $v\mapsto\int\psi v$ is bounded on $L^p$ by [[thm-holder-inequality-for-integrals]], and it commutes with the Bochner integral ([[thm-bounded-linear-maps-commute-with-bochner-integration]]). The iterated scalar integral is absolutely integrable against $\psi$, bounded by $T\|f\|_\infty\|\psi\|_1$, so Fubini ([[thm-tonelli-and-fubini-for-completed-product-measures]]) gives the same pairing for the scalar potential. Equality of all these pairings forces equality almost everywhere: on each bounded box, a positive or negative real or imaginary part of the difference on a measurable set of positive measure would give a nonzero pairing with that set's indicator.
items.strategy: Definition and well-definedness: Lp completeness makes the Bochner target Banach. Contraction and positive-time L1 kernel continuity give strong measurability via finite mesh approximations on an exhaustion avoiding the null endpoint for p=infinity. Simple forcing approximations give the finite-p L1-in-time variant. Bounded supported test pairings, Holder and absolute scalar Fubini identify scalar and Bochner potentials whenever both hypotheses hold. The empty time interval and zero forcing give zero; infinity continuity at the origin is not assumed.

items.title: L1 in time estimate for Lp Duhamel forcing
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $1\le p\le\infty$, and let
$f:[0,T]\to L^p(\mathbb R^n)$ be strongly measurable with
$\int_0^T\|f(s)\|_p\,ds<\infty$. For every $t$ the Bochner integral
$Df(t)=\int_0^tH_{t-s}f(s)\,ds$ exists and satisfies
$\|Df(t)\|_p\le\int_0^t\|f(s)\|_p\,ds$. For $p=\infty$ no strong continuity of
$H$ at zero on all $L^\infty$ is asserted. For merely weakly measurable
$L^\infty$ forcing this statement makes no existence assertion.
items.strategy: Statement and steps 1.1–4.1: for finite p, strong continuity and contraction give jointly continuous operator action; finite simple forcing values are approximated by finite meshes of their heat-flow curves. For infinity, the explicit derivative kernel has bounded L1 norm on positive-time compact intervals, so the same construction works on a countable exhaustion avoiding s=t. Diagonal mesh approximants converge off the original null set and the singleton endpoint. Banach completeness and contraction then prove Bochner existence and the exact L1-time estimate. At t=0 the empty integral is zero. Merely weakly measurable infinity forcing and infinity strong continuity at zero are expressly excluded.

items.title: Maximum principle on the whole space under Gaussian growth
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $T>0$, $a\ge0$, $A<\infty$, and let
$u\in C([0,T]\times\mathbb R^n)\cap C^{1,2}((0,T]\times\mathbb R^n)$ satisfy
$$u_t-\Delta u\le0,\qquad u(t,x)\le Ae^{a|x|^2}\quad((t,x)\in[0,T]\times\mathbb R^n).$$
Then
$$\sup_{[0,T]\times\mathbb R^n}u\le\sup_{\mathbb R^n}u(0,\cdot).$$
(The same statement holds for a finite union of consecutive strips of length
less than $1/(4a)$ when $a>0$.)
items.strategy: Statement and steps 1.1–4.1: the initial supremum may be infinite under Gaussian growth, and that case is explicitly immediate. For finite M, the positive barrier B=(T+delta-t)^(-n/2) exp(|x|^2/(4(T+delta-t))) satisfies Bt=Delta B and dominates the upper growth uniformly at infinity when aT<1/4. On positive-time truncated cylinders the checked bounded maximum principle applies; compact continuity sends the bottom error eta_h to zero without derivatives at zero. epsilon then tends to zero at a fixed point. Equal positive-length strips N>4aT handle every longer T and avoid degenerate last strips. a=0, negative A, n=1 and t=T are compatible; the two-sided bound is not required.

items.title: Uniqueness for the whole-space heat equation under Gaussian growth
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $T>0$, $C<\infty$, $a\ge0$, and let $u\in C([0,T]\times\mathbb R^n)\cap C^{1,2}((0,T]\times\mathbb R^n)$ satisfy $u_t-\Delta u=0$ on $\mathbb R^n\times(0,T)$, $u(0,\cdot)=0$ and
$$|u(t,x)|\le Ce^{a|x|^2}\qquad((t,x)\in[0,T]\times\mathbb R^n).$$
Then $u\equiv0$.
items.strategy: Apply [[lem-whole-space-maximum-principle-under-gaussian-growth]] to $u$: $u$ is a subsolution with $u(0,\cdot)\le0$, hence $u\le0$ on $[0,T]\times\mathbb R^n$. Applying the same lemma to $-u$, which is again a subsolution with $(-u)(0,\cdot)\le0$, gives $u\ge0$. When the strip length $T$ exceeds $1/(4a)$ the lemma is applied successively to the finitely many strips of length less than $1/(4a)$ covering $[0,T]$ (the growth hypothesis is inherited on each strip), which is the iteration referred to in the item title ([[thm-of-archimedean]] for the finiteness of the subdivision). Thus $u\equiv0$. Two applications and a finite subdivision only; Countable Choice is inherited from the supplier.

items.title: Duhamel principle for the whole-space heat equation
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice. (i) **Classical case.** Let $f$ be bounded and jointly
continuous on $\mathbb R^n\times[0,T]$, and suppose there are $C>0$ and
$0<\gamma\le1$ such that $|f(x,s)-f(y,s)|\le C|x-y|^\gamma$ for all $x,y$ and
$0\le s\le T$ (in particular smooth compactly supported forcing qualifies) and
define the scalar heat potential
$$u(t,x):=\int_0^t\int_{\mathbb R^n}\Gamma(x-y,t-s)f(y,s)\,dy\,ds .$$
Then $u\in C^{1,2}(\mathbb R^n\times(0,T])$, $u_t-\Delta u=f$ on
$\mathbb R^n\times(0,T)$ and $u(0,\cdot)=0$.

(ii) **Mild case.** Let $1\le p<\infty$ and $f\in C([0,T];L^p(\mathbb R^n))$.
Then $Df\in C([0,T];L^p(\mathbb R^n))$, $Df(0)=0$, and $Df$ satisfies the
forced semigroup relation
$$Df(t)=H_{t-s}Df(s)+\int_s^tH_{t-\tau}f(\tau)\,d\tau\qquad(0<s<t\le T).$$
Every element $w\in C([0,T];L^p(\mathbb R^n))$ with $w(0)=0$ satisfying this
relation equals $Df$. If moreover $|u(x,t)|\le Ce^{a|x|^2}$ for a classical
solution $u$ with zero initial data, then $u$ is the potential of (i) uniquely
in that growth class.
items.strategy: Statement (i),(ii) and steps 1.1–4.1: scalar forcing is bounded, jointly continuous and uniformly spatially gamma-Holder with gamma>0. Zeroth and first derivative integrals have bounds M and C M tau^(-1/2); second derivatives use zero kernel mass and subtract f(x,s), giving the integrable cancellation bound C tau^(-1+gamma/2). Positive-depth cutoffs and the exact uniform derivative-limit theorem justify the spatial derivatives. The moving-endpoint time derivative is Gamma_delta*f(t-delta)+int Delta Gamma*f, which converges locally uniformly to f+Delta u, including the left endpoint convention at T. The original uncancelled second-derivative double integral is not asserted to be absolutely integrable: cancellation bounds the inner integral's value. Mild continuity uses Bochner dominated convergence for both-sided t limits; splitting and bounded-map commutation prove the relation, and contraction as s decreases to zero proves uniqueness. Classical difference uniqueness uses the stated continuous initial trace and uniform Gaussian growth. The clause only proves C^{1,2}, not full smoothness for continuous time forcing.

items.title: The inhomogeneous heat Cauchy formula
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge1$, $T>0$, $1\le p<\infty$,
$u_0\in L^p(\mathbb R^n)$ and $f\in C([0,T];L^p(\mathbb R^n))$. Define
$$u(t):=H_tu_0+Df(t)=H_tu_0+\int_0^tH_{t-s}f(s)\,ds\qquad(0\le t\le T).$$
Then $u\in C([0,T];L^p(\mathbb R^n))$, $u(0)=u_0$, and $u$ satisfies the forced
relation
$$u(t)=H_{t-s}u(s)+\int_s^tH_{t-\tau}f(\tau)\,d\tau\qquad(0<s<t\le T);$$
conversely every $w\in C([0,T];L^p(\mathbb R^n))$ with $w(0)=u_0$ satisfying this
relation equals $u$. If $u_0$ is bounded and uniformly continuous and $f$ is
bounded and jointly continuous and uniformly spatially Hölder on $[0,T]$ as in
the Duhamel theorem, then $u$ is a classical solution of $u_t-\Delta u=f$ with
$u(\cdot,0)=u_0$, and it is the unique classical solution in the Gaussian
growth class. For bounded uniformly continuous $u_0$ and bounded jointly
uniformly continuous $f$ without the Hölder assumption, the same scalar formula
remains a bounded continuous mild solution with the forced semigroup relation
and initial trace $u_0$; the $C^{1,2}$ upgrade is not claimed for that general
forcing class.
items.strategy: Statement and steps 1.1–3.1: finite-p strong heat continuity plus Duhamel continuity gives the mild formula and initial class; splitting and the semigroup law give its forced relation. Conversely the difference contracts against its initial limit zero. The classical clause separately assumes bounded uniformly continuous initial data and bounded continuous spatially Holder forcing, so the checked homogeneous and Duhamel suppliers yield the PDE and Gaussian-class uniqueness. For bounded uniformly continuous forcing without Holder regularity, a scalar dominated-convergence argument supplies only a bounded continuous mild solution; absolute kernel-mass estimates justify signed/complex Fubini for its relation. No unjustified C^{1,2} upgrade is made in that last clause.

items.title: Instantaneous smoothing of the Lp heat flow
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice, let $n\ge1$, $1\le p\le q\le\infty$ and let $Q$ be the Young exponent of [[thm-lp-to-lq-heat-kernel-estimate]]. For every $f\in L^p(\mathbb R^n)$ the integral representative
$$u(x,t):=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\Gamma(x-y,t)f(y)\,dy$$
is $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R^n\times(0,\infty)$ and satisfies $u_t=\Delta u$ there; moreover for every multi-index $\alpha$ and every integer $m\ge0$,
$$D_x^\alpha\partial_t^mu=(\Delta_x^mD_x^\alpha\Gamma_t)*f,\qquad \|D_x^\alpha\partial_t^mu(\cdot,t)\|_q\le C_{n,\alpha,m,Q}\,t^{-\frac{2m+|\alpha|}{2}-\frac n2(\frac1p-\frac1q)}\|f\|_p$$
for every $t>0$, with $C_{n,\alpha,m,Q}$ the constant produced by the derivative bounds of [[lem-spatial-and-time-derivatives-pass-through-heat-convolution-for-positive-time]] and [[thm-lp-to-lq-heat-kernel-estimate]]. No strong continuity of $H_tf$ at $t=0$ is asserted for $q=\infty$ or $p=\infty$.
items.strategy: This assembles the positive-time smoothing statements of the heat-kernel page. The identity $\partial_t^k\Gamma_t=\Delta_x^k\Gamma_t$ holds because $\Gamma$ solves the heat equation and is $C^\infty$ for positive time, and the derivative pass-through lemma [[lem-spatial-and-time-derivatives-pass-through-heat-convolution-for-positive-time]] gives $D_x^\alpha\partial_t^ku=(D_x^\alpha\partial_t^k\Gamma_t)*f$ with the Gaussian derivative bound $|D_x^\alpha\partial_t^k\Gamma(x,t)|\le C t^{-(n+|\alpha|+2k)/2}e^{-|x|^2/8t}$; in particular every derivative integral converges and $u$ is $C^\infty$ with $u_t=\Delta u$ ([[lem-spatial-and-time-derivatives-pass-through-heat-convolution-for-positive-time]], [[lem-heat-kernel-normalisation-scaling-and-derivatives]]). The $L^q$ bound is Young's estimate [[thm-lp-to-lq-heat-kernel-estimate]] applied to the kernel $D_x^\alpha\partial_t^m\Gamma_t$, whose $L^Q$ norm scales as $t^{-\frac{2m+|\alpha|}{2}}$, multiplied by the scaling factor $t^{-\frac n2(\frac1p-\frac1q)}$; this is exactly the estimate of [[thm-spatial-derivative-estimates-for-heat-flow]] extended to time derivatives by the identity. The caveat records that positive-time smoothing does not give strong continuity at zero in the supremum norm ([[def-heat-evolution-of-initial-data]], [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]] for the multi-index notation).

items.title: Spatial smoothing of forcing separated from the observation time
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $1\le p\le q\le\infty$,
$f\in L^1([0,T];L^p(\mathbb R^n))$ in the Bochner sense,
$0<\varepsilon\le t\le T$, and suppose $f(s)=0$ for almost every
$s>t-\varepsilon$. Then the Duhamel contribution at $t$ has a spatial
$C^\infty$ representative, and for every multi-index $\alpha$,
$$D^\alpha Df(t)=\int_0^{t-\varepsilon}D^\alpha H_{t-s}f(s)\,ds\qquad\text{with}\qquad\|D^\alpha Df(t)\|_q\le C_{\alpha,n,p,q}\,\varepsilon^{-\frac{|\alpha|}{2}-\frac n2(\frac1p-\frac1q)}\int_0^{t-\varepsilon}\|f(s)\|_p\,ds .$$
This asserts spatial regularity at the chosen time, not differentiability across
an active forcing time diagonal.
items.strategy: Statement and steps 1.1–3.1: take a=epsilon/2 and g=int_0^(t-epsilon) H_(t-s-a) f(s). The integrability theorem applies to cut-off forcing at t-a, and the bounded-map Bochner identity gives Df(t)=H_a g. Thus no joint representative selection is needed. The bounded derivative map Lp->Lq commutes with that integral; equality of the smooth semigroup representatives supplies the derivative identity. Since t-s>=epsilon, the derivative estimate yields the exact epsilon power. t=epsilon gives zero; p=q=infinity and alpha=0 work, with no time regularity across active forcing asserted.

items.title: The complex-time heat kernel on a proper sector
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Fix $n\ge1$ and
$\theta\in(0,\pi/2)$ and put
$S_\theta:=\{z\in\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}:|\arg z|<\theta\}$. For $z\in S_\theta$
and $x\in\mathbb R^n$ define the **complex-time heat kernel**
$$\Gamma_z(x):=(4\pi z)^{-n/2}\exp\Bigl(-\frac{|x|^2}{4z}\Bigr),$$
where $(4\pi z)^{-n/2}:=\exp\bigl(-\frac n2\operatorname{Log}(4\pi z)\bigr)$ with
the principal logarithm. This is legitimate: $z\ne0$ and
$\operatorname{Re}(4\pi z)=4\pi|z|\cos(\arg z)>0$ because $|\arg z|<\theta<\pi/2$,
so $4\pi z$ lies in the slit plane on which the principal logarithm is
holomorphic ([[cor-principal-logarithm-is-holomorphic-on-the-slit-plane]],
[[def-complex-power-from-holomorphic-logarithm-branch]]) and the power is the
complex exponential of [[def-complex-exponential]]. Then:

(i) $\Gamma_z\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^n)\cap L^1(\mathbb R^n)$ and
$\int_{\mathbb R^n}\Gamma_z(x)\,dx=1$;

(ii) for every $\sigma\in(0,\theta)$ and every $z$ with $|\arg z|\le\sigma$,
$\ \|\Gamma_z\|_1\le(\cos\sigma)^{-n/2}$;

(iii) for real $z=t>0$, $\Gamma_t$ is the heat kernel of [[def-heat-kernel]];

(iv) for every fixed $x$ the map $z\mapsto\Gamma_z(x)$ is holomorphic on
$S_\theta$ with
$\partial_z\Gamma_z(x)=\bigl(-\tfrac n{2z}+\tfrac{|x|^2}{4z^2}\bigr)\Gamma_z(x)$;

(v) for every compact $K\Subset S_\theta$ there are constants $c_K,C_K>0$ with
$|\Gamma_z(x)|\le C_Ke^{-c_K|x|^2}$ and
$|\partial_z\Gamma_z(x)|\le C_K(1+|x|^2)e^{-c_K|x|^2}$ for all $z\in K$,
$x\in\mathbb R^n$.

The complex exponential is entire with derivative itself ([[thm-complex-exponential-is-entire-with-derivative-itself]]), and the complex chain rule is [[thm-chain-rule-for-complex-derivatives]]. Its modulus is $|e^w|=e^{\operatorname{Re}w}$ ([[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]). Smoothness in (i) follows by repeated coordinate differentiation of the exponential and
power on $\mathbb R^n$ ([[thm-algebra-of-complex-derivatives]],
[[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-chain-rule]],
[[def-complex-differentiability-holomorphic-and-entire]]); square-integrability
and the exponential bound in (v) follow from
$\operatorname{Re}(1/z)=\cos(\arg z)/|z|>0$ together with the compactness of
$K$ and the growth of the exponential against polynomials
([[thm-exponential-beats-every-polynomial]], [[thm-heine-borel-rn]],
[[def-metric-compactness]]). The remaining assertions are justified in the
reminders below.
items.strategy: Definition (i)–(v) and all three remarks: the principal branch is legitimate on the right half-plane; the modulus integrates to (cos arg z)^(-n/2). Truncated one-dimensional Gaussian integrals are holomorphic, their tails converge locally uniformly, and the scalar identity theorem plus absolutely integrable product Fubini supplies mass one. Log(1/(4z))=-Log(4z) on this sector fixes branch cancellation. Compact parameter sets bound |z| above and away from zero and Re(1/z) away from zero. No claim at z=0 or sector angle pi/2.

items.title: The complex-time heat kernel is L1-differentiable in its parameter
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $\theta\in(0,\pi/2)$ and let $\Gamma_z$ be the
complex-time heat kernel of
[[def-complex-time-heat-kernel-on-a-proper-sector]]. Then for every
$z\in S_\theta$ the complex difference quotients converge in
$L^1(\mathbb R^n)$:
$$\Bigl\|\frac{\Gamma_{z+h}-\Gamma_z}{h}-\partial_z\Gamma_z\Bigr\|_1\longrightarrow0\qquad(h\to0),$$
so $z\mapsto\Gamma_z$ is complex differentiable on $S_\theta$ with values in
$L^1(\mathbb R^n)$ and derivative $\partial_z\Gamma_z$. The convergence is
uniform on compact subsets of $S_\theta$.
items.strategy: Statement and steps 1.1–3.1: componentwise FTC gives the segment integral identity and the derivative majorant on a larger compact K+. The derivative is uniformly continuous there for each x, and the compact-parameter supremum is a measurable continuous function of x, dominated by an integrable polynomial Gaussian. Dominated convergence proves both L1 differentiation and compact-uniform convergence. Amended step 2.1 to permit all 0<|h|<d instead of incorrectly requiring z+h in arbitrary K (which may be a singleton); closed defect f39-b1-compact-increment-domain. No Statement change.

items.title: Complex-time heat operators form a bounded holomorphic semigroup
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $\theta\in(0,\pi/2)$ and $1\le p\le\infty$. For
$z\in S_\theta$ and $f\in L^p(\mathbb R^n)$ define
$$H_zf:=\Gamma_z*f,$$
the convolution with the complex-time kernel of
[[def-complex-time-heat-kernel-on-a-proper-sector]]. Then:

(i) $H_z$ is a bounded operator on $L^p(\mathbb R^n)$ with
$\|H_z\|_{L^p\to L^p}\le(\cos\sigma)^{-n/2}$ whenever
$|\arg z|\le\sigma<\theta$;

(ii) $H_zH_w=H_{z+w}$ whenever $z,w,z+w\in S_\theta$;

(iii) for every $f$ the map $z\mapsto H_zf$ is complex differentiable on
$S_\theta$ in the norm of $L^p(\mathbb R^n)$, with derivative
$(\partial_z\Gamma_z)*f$; consequently $z\mapsto H_z$ is holomorphic in
operator norm on every proper subsector $S_\sigma$, $\sigma<\theta$.
items.strategy: Statement and steps 1.1–3.1: Young supplies boundedness for all p. The sector is an open convex cone, closed under addition. Pairing the L1 kernel difference quotients with a bounded fixed kernel gives scalar holomorphy; the real Gaussian convolution law extends first in z and then in w by two scalar identity-theorem applications on the connected sector. Iterated absolute kernels have the required Lp bound, so Fubini gives operator composition also at p=1,infinity. The L1 derivative error uniformly bounds the operator-norm error over ||f||p<=1, proving operator holomorphy. No complex translation of the spatial contour is used and z=0 is outside scope.

items.title: The heat operator family is an analytic semigroup in the later abstract language
items.statement:
**Orientation only.** For $1\le p<\infty$, the family $z\mapsto H_z$ constructed explicitly in
[[thm-complex-time-heat-operators-form-a-bounded-holomorphic-semigroup]] is the
concrete Gaussian instance of what the library's later abstract treatment of
analytic semigroups will call a bounded holomorphic (analytic) $C_0$-semigroup
on a sector: bounded on every proper subsector, strongly continuous on the
positive real axis, and multiplicative in the sector. Concretely, the kernel
and its estimates are those of [[def-complex-time-heat-kernel-on-a-proper-sector]];
the sectorial bound $\|H_z\|_{L^p\to L^p}\le(\cos\sigma)^{-n/2}$ on
$|\arg z|\le\sigma<\theta$ and the law $H_zH_w=H_{z+w}$ are clauses (i) and
(ii) of that theorem, its clause (iii) gives the holomorphy in operator norm,
and the strong continuity at the vertex along the positive axis, for
$1\le p<\infty$, is that of the heat flow of
[[def-heat-evolution-of-initial-data]] supplied by
[[thm-heat-cauchy-solution-for-lp-data]].

This page does not use that abstract notion as a premise, does not identify the
generator $\Delta$ with an unbounded operator domain, and makes no claim about
maximal regularity, resolvent sectors, or the Hille–Yosida representation in
the abstract language. The later page is responsible for the abstract
definition and for the generator theory; here only the explicit kernel family
of [[def-complex-time-heat-kernel-on-a-proper-sector]] and its estimates are
used.

For $p=\infty$ the same family is bounded and operator-norm holomorphic at positive complex times, but is not a $C_0$-semigroup on all of $L^\infty$; the vertex continuity assertion above is restricted to finite $p$. Indeed, for $f=\mathbf1_{[0,\infty)}$ on $\mathbb R$, evenness and unit mass give $H_tf(0)=1/2$. Continuity of $H_tf$ makes $|H_tf(x)-1|>\eta$ on a positive-length interval $0<x<\delta$ for every $\eta<1/2$; hence $\|H_tf-f\|_\infty\ge1/2$ for every $t>0$.

For finite $p$, continuity at the vertex also holds within each proper subsector. With $\varepsilon>0$ real and $|\arg z|\le\sigma$, the semigroup law gives
$$\|H_zf-f\|_p\le((\cos\sigma)^{-n/2}+1)\|f-H_\varepsilon f\|_p+\|H_{z+\varepsilon}f-H_\varepsilon f\|_p.$$
For fixed $\varepsilon$, the last term tends to zero as $z\to0$ by positive-parameter operator holomorphy; then $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ controls the first term by the finite-$p$ real-time continuity cited above. This supplies the vertex continuity of the analytic $C_0$ terminology.
items.strategy: All remark paragraphs: finite-p real-time strong continuity, sector multiplication and operator-norm holomorphy provide the stated concrete analytic C0 interpretation. Approximate f by H_epsilon f to get vertex continuity in every proper subsector; fixed epsilon positive-time holomorphy controls the residual. For p=infinity the half-line indicator is legitimate infinity data, and continuity near zero gives a positive-length set of norm discrepancy at least any eta<1/2, hence essential norm at least 1/2. No generator domain or abstract regularity premise is used.

items.title: L2 normalisation of the sine modes on an interval
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice. For all integers $k,l\ge1$,
$$\int_0^\pi\sin(kx)\sin(lx)\,dx=\frac\pi2\,\delta_{kl}.$$
In particular $\|\sin(k\cdot)\|_{L^2(0,\pi)}=\sqrt{\pi/2}$.
items.strategy: Statement and steps 1.1–4.1: product-to-sum separates k=l (zero difference frequency) from k!=l (nonzero frequencies, possibly negative). The primitive sin(mx)/m and sine endpoint zeros evaluate every nonzero frequency; the constant frequency integrates to pi. Thus the orthogonality integral is pi/2 delta_kl and the quotient norm is sqrt(pi/2). Countable Choice is explicitly carried through the Hilbert-space dictionary only; k=l=1 is included.

items.title: The backward heat solution map is unbounded
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $T>0$ and consider the heat equation
$u_t=u_{xx}$ on $(0,\pi)\times(0,T]$ with homogeneous Dirichlet boundary data
$u(0,t)=u(\pi,t)=0$.

**Well-definedness of the terminal-to-initial map.** If a $C^{4,2}$ function $w$
on $[0,\pi]\times[0,T]$ solves this problem with $w(x,T)=0$ for all $x$, then
$w\equiv0$
([[lem-backward-uniqueness-for-the-heat-equation-on-a-bounded-interval]]). Hence
on the class of $C^{4,2}$ solutions the terminal data determine the solution, and
the map $S$ sending a terminal datum $u(\cdot,T)$ to the initial state
$u(\cdot,0)$ is well defined.

**Unboundedness.** For every integer $k\ge1$ the function
$$u_k(x,t):=e^{k^2(T-t)}\sin(kx)$$
is a classical solution of $u_t=u_{xx}$ on $(0,\pi)\times(0,T]$ with
$u_k(0,t)=u_k(\pi,t)=0$, initial state $u_k(\cdot,0)=e^{k^2T}\sin(k\cdot)$ and
terminal data $u_k(\cdot,T)=\sin(k\cdot)$. Consequently there is no constant
$C<\infty$ with
$$\|u(\cdot,0)\|_{L^2(0,\pi)}\le C\,\|u(\cdot,T)\|_{L^2(0,\pi)}$$
for all $C^{4,2}$ solutions $u$ of this problem: the solutions
$\tilde u_k(x,t)=e^{-k^2t}\sin(kx)$ have terminal data
$g_k=e^{-k^2T}\sin(k\cdot)$ with
$\|g_k\|_2=\sqrt{\pi/2}\,e^{-k^2T}\to0$ while
$\|\tilde u_k(\cdot,0)\|_2=\sqrt{\pi/2}$ for every $k$. Since
$Sg_k=\sin(k\cdot)=e^{k^2T}g_k$, the terminal-to-initial map multiplies the
$k$-th sine mode by $e^{k^2T}$ and is unbounded with respect to the
$L^2(0,\pi)$ norms on its domain and range: the backward heat problem on a
bounded interval has no norm-stable solution operator, and the amplification
factor of the $k$-th Dirichlet mode is exactly $e^{k^2T}$.
items.strategy: Statement and steps 1.1–3.1: subtracting C^{4,2} solutions invokes the fully checked backward uniqueness lemma, so the terminal map is single valued on its actual attained-data domain. The smooth modes exp(k^2(T-t)) sin(kx) have both derivatives -k^2 times the mode and zero lateral values. The decaying modes give norm ratio exp(k^2 T), terminal norms tending to zero and initial norm sqrt(pi/2). This disproves every finite inverse bound while making no existence assertion for arbitrary infinite data. T>0 and Countable Choice are explicit.

items.title: Compactly supported nonzero terminal profiles are outside the heat range
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge1$, $1\le p\le\infty$, $f\in L^p(\mathbb R^n)$
and $t>0$, and let $u$ be the everywhere-defined representative of the heat
evolution $H_tf$ supplied by
[[thm-positive-time-spatial-analyticity-of-heat-kernel-solutions]]. If $u$ has
compact support, then $u\equiv0$ and $H_tf=0$ as an element of
$L^p(\mathbb R^n)$. Consequently no nonzero compactly supported element of
$L^p(\mathbb R^n)$ equals $H_tf$ for any such $f$ and $t$. The same vanishing
conclusion holds when $u$ vanishes almost everywhere outside some compact set.
items.strategy: Statement and steps 1.1–6.1: the analyticity supplier gives global convergence along the fixed e1 line, so the real one-variable identity theorem applies to both components. Compact support makes a nonempty open zero interval. The box-volume supplier proves continuous versus almost-everywhere vanishing outside a compact set. Zero data, n=1, p=1 and p=infinity are covered; no injectivity of heat flow is claimed.

items.title: Backward ill-posedness does not mean universal nonexistence
items.statement:
**Orientation only.** Assume Countable Choice and fix $T>0$.
[[thm-backward-heat-solution-map-is-unbounded]] shows that the terminal-to-initial
map on the terminal profiles of $C^{4,2}$ interval Dirichlet heat solutions is
unbounded with respect to the $L^2(0,\pi)$ norms; this is a statement
about continuity and stability, not about existence. The terminal data
$\sin(k\cdot)$, for integers $k\ge1$, do have backward solutions (the modes $u_k$ of
[[thm-backward-heat-solution-map-is-unbounded]]), and so does every finite sine
sum, by finite linear combination of these solutions. More generally, whenever
a forward interval Dirichlet heat solution $u$ exists on $[0,T]$ with initial
profile $f$, its terminal profile $g=u(\cdot,T)$ admits a backward extension
on that interval: the same $u$, with initial profile $f$. This range description
asserts no existence for arbitrary initial or terminal data. The failure is therefore
that arbitrarily small terminal perturbations can correspond to order-one
initial states ([[thm-backward-heat-solution-map-is-unbounded]]), and on general
domains the backward solution operator need not be surjective onto any given
data class. No claim of universal nonexistence and no well-posedness claim is
made here.

The well-definedness half of the picture is also worth recording: on the $C^{4,2}$
class with zero lateral data the terminal data determine the solution, by
[[lem-backward-uniqueness-for-the-heat-equation-on-a-bounded-interval]], so
ill-posedness here is exactly the failure of a uniform norm bound, with the
amplification ratio $e^{k^2T}$ of the $k$-th sine mode
([[lem-ltwo-normalisation-of-sine-modes-on-the-interval]]) measuring that
failure; no further existence or regularity claim is made.
items.strategy: Assume Countable Choice and T>0. On terminal profiles of C^{4,2} interval Dirichlet heat solutions, backward uniqueness supplies a well-defined inverse; explicit sine modes and their finite linear combinations supply existence examples, and the factor exp(k^2 T) gives unboundedness. Every attained forward interval terminal profile has its own forward history as a backward extension. No arbitrary-data existence is asserted; whole-space H_t is not used.

items.title: Duhamel solution for a time-independent source
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge1$, $1\le p<\infty$, $T>0$ and let
$f\in L^p(\mathbb R^n)$ be viewed as the time-independent source
$f(x,t):=f(x)$; if $f$ is spatially Hölder continuous with compact support,
read the classical statement below. The heat potential of
[[def-duhamel-heat-potential]] is
$$Df(t)=\int_0^tH_{t-s}f\,ds=\int_0^tH_\tau f\,d\tau,$$
the substitution $\tau=t-s$ removing the time dependence. Then
$Df\in C([0,T];L^p(\mathbb R^n))$, $Df(0)=0$, and in the classical compactly
supported case $(Df)_t-\Delta Df=f$ on $\mathbb R^n\times(0,T]$. In particular
$Df$ is the solution of the inhomogeneous Cauchy problem with zero initial data
produced by the Duhamel principle, and for a time-independent source the two
representations $\int_0^tH_{t-s}f\,ds$ and $\int_0^tH_\tau f\,d\tau$ agree.
items.strategy: Example and steps 1.1–3.1: a fixed finite-p datum is a continuous forcing curve. Reflection s->t-s preserves the simple-integral measures and hence both Bochner representations agree. In the compactly supported globally Holder case the bounded jointly continuous uniform spatial-Holder hypotheses of the checked Duhamel theorem hold, and scalar/Bochner agreement from the definition supplies the representative. Positive-time derivative continuity extends the equation to T. Zero forcing and t=0 give zero; no unbounded Laplacian commutation for arbitrary Lp data is asserted. items.title: Heat comparison preserves an interval of values
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice. Let $Q=\Omega\times(0,T]$ be a parabolic cylinder with $\Omega$ bounded, let $a\le b$ be real constants, and let $u\in C^{2,1}(\overline Q)$ solve $u_t-\Delta u=0$ in $Q$ with $a\le u\le b$ on the parabolic boundary $\partial_pQ$. Then $a\le u\le b$ on all of $\overline Q$. On the whole space the analogous statement is that $a\le u_0\le b$ almost everywhere implies $a\le H_tu_0\le b$ almost everywhere for every $t>0$.
items.strategy: The constant functions $a$ and $b$ are solutions of the heat equation in $Q$ with the same value on all of $\overline Q$. Apply the comparison principle of [[cor-comparison-and-uniqueness-for-the-bounded-cylinder-heat-problem]](i) to the pair $(a,u)$: $a_t-\Delta a=0=u_t-\Delta u$ and $a\le u$ on $\partial_pQ$, hence $a\le u$ on $\overline Q$; the same with $(u,b)$ gives $u\le b$. The whole-space statement is the order preservation and constant preservation of the heat flow ([[cor-heat-flow-is-order-preserving-and-lp-contractive]], [[cor-heat-flow-preserves-mass-and-positivity]], [[def-heat-evolution-of-initial-data]]). No further choice is used.

items.title: Sine modes decay under Dirichlet heat flow
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice. For every integer $k\ge1$ and every $T>0$, the function
$$u_k(x,t):=e^{-k^2t}\sin(kx)$$
is a classical solution of the heat equation $u_t=\Delta u$ on
$(0,\pi)\times(0,T]$ with Dirichlet data $u_k(0,t)=u_k(\pi,t)=0$ and initial
data $u_k(x,0)=\sin(kx)$; it is smooth up to $t=0$ in this one-dimensional
setting. Its $L^2(0,\pi)$ norm decays at the rate of the $k$-th Dirichlet
eigenvalue,
$$\|u_k(\cdot,t)\|_2=e^{-k^2t}\sqrt{\pi/2}\qquad(t\ge0),$$
so higher modes decay faster, and the nodal set of $u_k(\cdot,t)$ does not
depend on $t$.
items.strategy: Example and steps 1.1–4.1: exp(-k^2 t) sin(kx) solves the forward equation smoothly on the closed rectangle, with named spatial-first boundary and initial slots. The squared L2 norm is exp(-2k^2 t) pi/2, and the exponential never vanishes so the nodal set is {m pi/k:1<=m<=k-1}. For k=1 that set is empty. Faster decay is asserted only at positive time; Countable Choice is carried through the norm supplier.

items.title: The final-time face is not part of the parabolic boundary
items.statement:
The claim refuted is that every supersolution $u_t-\Delta u\ge0$ on a bounded cylinder $Q$ satisfies $\max_{\overline Q}u\le\max_{\partial_pQ}u$. The witness has its larger maximum at a spatially interior point of the final-time face, which is excluded from the parabolic boundary. Take $\Omega=(0,\pi)$ and
$$u(x,t):=e^{t}\sin x .$$
Then $u_t=e^t\sin x$ and $\Delta u=-e^t\sin x$, so
$u_t-\Delta u=2e^t\sin x\ge0$ in $Q$: $u$ is a supersolution. Its maximum over
the closed cylinder is $\max_{\overline Q}u=e^{T}$, attained at the interior
point $(\pi/2,T)$ of the final-time face, whereas
$$\max_{\partial_pQ}u=\max\Bigl(\max_{[0,\pi]}\sin,0\Bigr)=1<e^{T}$$
because the lateral data vanish and the initial data are $\sin x\le1$ with
equality at $x=\pi/2$. So the final-time face is not part of the parabolic
boundary, and for a supersolution the maximum over the cylinder is genuinely
larger than the parabolic-boundary maximum: the maximum principle is
sign-sensitive and does not extend in the reverse direction.
items.strategy: Statement refuted and steps 1.1–3.1: u=exp(t) sin x is a supersolution, with zero lateral data, parabolic-boundary maximum one and cylinder maximum exp(T)>1 at (pi/2,T). This refutes the written supersolution maximum bound. It cannot refute an equality with a boundary enlarged to include that face, which the reader reports was the original mistaken target. The current text instead distinguishes the valid supersolution minimum principle and verifies the ordinary subsolution maximum principle for -u. T>0 and the spatial slots are correct.

items.title: Incompatible initial and boundary values prevent corner continuity
items.statement:
The claim refuted is that the interval Dirichlet heat problem on
$(0,\pi)\times(0,T]$ with initial data $u(x,0)=1$ for $0<x<\pi$ and lateral data
$u(0,t)=u(\pi,t)=0$ for $t>0$ can be solved by a function $u$ that is
continuous on $[0,\pi]\times[0,T]$ and attains its data: no such continuous
function exists, because the two prescriptions disagree at the corners.
items.strategy: Statement refuted and steps 1.1–3.1: for every T>0, (1/(k+1),0) lies in the initial face and (0,T/(k+1)) lies in the lateral face. Both approach the same corner with prescribed values one and zero. Continuity contradicts those limits without any PDE existence prerequisite. The scaled lateral sequence works also when T<1; data are only imposed off the corner.

items.title: Tychonoff nonuniqueness: zero-data heat solutions without growth control (recorded, not proved here)
items.statement: **Recorded orientation, not proved here.** The growth hypothesis in [[thm-whole-space-heat-uniqueness-under-gaussian-growth]] cannot be dropped: for the one-dimensional heat equation $u_t=u_{xx}$ there exist nonzero smooth solutions on $\mathbb R\times(0,\infty)$ with $u(0,x)=0$ for all $x$. Teschl's Example 6.4 writes $u(t,x)=\sum_{m\ge0}\varphi^{(m)}(t)x^{2m}/(2m)!$ with $\varphi(t)=e^{-1/t^2}$ for $t>0$ and $\varphi(t)=0$ for $t\le0$; the series converges for every $x$ and solves the heat equation with vanishing initial data. Hunter's Example 5.7 records the same construction and notes that the resulting solution grows very rapidly as $|x|\to\infty$. Such solutions are therefore outside every Gaussian growth class and do not contradict the uniqueness theorem above; the statement of the recorded result is not proved on this page.
items.strategy: Recorded, not proved here; the proof obligation is discharged externally. This remark carries no local proof, is a leaf, and no item of this page depends on it.

items.title: Backward heat amplifies small high-frequency errors
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice. The claim refuted is that the backward heat problem on $(0,\pi)$ depends
continuously on its terminal data in the $L^2(0,\pi)$ norm: arbitrarily small
terminal perturbations do not, in general, produce small perturbations of the
initial state.
items.strategy: Statement refuted and steps 1.1–3.1: the current sine mode example and backward uniqueness/unboundedness theorem justify explicit admissible terminal pairs and a single-valued inverse on their attained-data class. The norm computation gives ||gk||2=sqrt(pi/2) exp(-k^2 T)->0 and ||Sgk||2=sqrt(pi/2), proving discontinuity at zero relative to that domain. Countable Choice and T>0 are explicit. This is failure of stability; it makes no false claim of nonexistence.

items.title: Finite sine sums admit a backward Dirichlet heat solution
items.statement:
For $T>0$ and a finite terminal sine sum
$g(x)=\sum_{k=1}^Na_k\sin(kx)$ on $(0,\pi)$, the function
$$u(x,t)=\sum_{k=1}^Na_ke^{k^2(T-t)}\sin(kx)\qquad(0\le t\le T)$$
solves $u_t-u_{xx}=0$, vanishes at $x=0$ and $x=\pi$, and has $u(x,T)=g(x)$.
Every such finite terminal datum therefore has a classical backward extension,
although its mode amplification grows without bound as $k$ increases.
items.strategy: Example and steps 1.1–3.1: each summand ak exp(k^2(T-t)) sin(kx) is smooth, has time and second spatial derivatives -k^2 times itself, vanishes at x=0,pi and attains its terminal term at T. Finite summation preserves all conditions. Zero coefficients yield the zero solution, and an empty sum would do the same; the written Given chooses N>=1. No convergence or existence assertion for infinite sums is made.

items.title: A mild heat solution need not be classical at the initial time
items.statement:
The claim refuted is that a mild $L^p$ solution of the heat equation is
automatically a classical solution continuous up to $t=0$, so that its
representative tends to the initial datum at the initial time pointwise.
items.strategy: Statement refuted and steps 1.1–2.1: 1_[0,1] has every finite-p norm one and belongs to infinity; this repairs the reader-reported half-line finite-p error. Heat scaling gives u(0,t)=int_0^(1/sqrt(t)) Gamma(z,1), tending to 1/2. More strongly, any continuous representative of its class would equal zero on (-infinity,0) and one on (0,1), by the positive-volume interval argument, so cannot be continuous at zero. This refutes a jointly continuous extension independently of null-set conventions. Only finite-p norm convergence is asserted.
